forces.title: AI Accelerates Early Drug Discovery Timelines Significantly
forces.description: Artificial intelligence is demonstrably compressing early drug discovery timelines, with first-in-human or equivalent preclinical milestones achieved 15 to 80 percent faster than large pharma medians. This acceleration is evident across various modalities and target novelties. While definitive Phase III efficacy readouts for AI-originated molecules are still years away, the initial speed gains are a strong tailwind for the Life Sciences Tools, CRDMO & Research sector, particularly for companies leveraging AI in early-stage research.
forces.source_title: AI drug discovery: Focusing on what matters most

forces.title: Biological Bottleneck in Target Identification Hampers Drug Discovery
forces.description: The industry's core constraint in drug discovery is the biological bottleneck of identifying and validating the right disease mechanism, target, biomarker, or patient population. Getting this wrong leads to clinical trial failures, even with well-optimized molecules. AI models currently struggle to distinguish true biological causality from mere statistical association in sparse, heterogeneous data, highlighting a critical risk that undercuts the potential of AI investments concentrated elsewhere in the value chain.
forces.source_title: AI drug discovery: Focusing on what matters most

forces.title: Low AI Maturity Persists in Preclinical and Translational Research
forces.description: Preclinical and translational research remains the least mature domain for AI application in drug discovery. Modeling systemic toxicity and off-target effects is vastly more complex than predicting binding affinity, due to species differences, variable disease models, and sparse human-linked data. Consequently, about one-quarter of Phase II and Phase III failures stem from unpredicted safety issues. This immaturity acts as a significant headwind, requiring substantial internal investment in predictive safety pipelines and proprietary data engines.
forces.source_title: AI drug discovery: Focusing on what matters most

forces.title: Regulatory Support for AI and NAMs in Toxicity Models
forces.description: Regulatory bodies are increasingly supportive of advanced computational tools in drug development. The FDA announced plans in April 2025 to rely more on AI-based toxicity models and New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), such as human organoids, to reduce dependence on traditional animal testing. This building regulatory support provides a significant tailwind for the development and adoption of AI tools and platforms focused on preclinical safety and toxicity prediction within the Life Sciences Tools and Research sector.
forces.source_title: AI drug discovery: Focusing on what matters most

forces.title: Biopharma Manufacturing Productivity Gains Have Plateaued
forces.description: After a decade of strong cost improvements and productivity gains (up 25% from 2014-2018), momentum in biopharma manufacturing has stalled. Since 2018, productivity has declined by 5%, and unit costs have largely plateaued. This saturation of traditional improvement levers acts as a headwind for CDMOs, increasing pressure to find new sources of performance amidst declining net prices for branded drugs and structurally more complex manufacturing requirements.
forces.source_title: Backbones and networks: A blueprint for the biopharma plant of the future

forces.title: Digital and AI are Top Agenda for Biomanufacturing Efficiency
forces.description: Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence have moved to the top of the agenda for biopharma manufacturers seeking new sources of performance. This reflects a structural shift in how companies aim to address plateauing productivity, increasing complexity, and declining drug prices. While many companies are initiating digital and AI journeys, the widespread prioritization of these technologies creates a tailwind for providers of advanced manufacturing tools, data platforms, and automation solutions within the CDMO space.
forces.source_title: Backbones and networks: A blueprint for the biopharma plant of the future

forces.title: Scaling Challenges for Digital/AI Pilots in Biopharma Manufacturing
forces.description: A significant challenge for biopharma manufacturers is that too few digital and AI pilot efforts have translated into scaled operational impact. Approximately two-thirds of companies remain in exploration or targeted implementation stages, with only a small minority fully embedding AI across operations. This creates a key risk of fragmented changes that improve individual steps without transforming the overall manufacturing system, leading to internal 'swirl' rather than competitive advantage for CDMOs and their technology partners.
forces.source_title: Backbones and networks: A blueprint for the biopharma plant of the future

forces.title: Rising Complexity and Delays Plague Clinical Trials
forces.description: Clinical trials are facing persistent challenges due to increasing complexity, with most respondents expecting this trend to continue. The share of trials experiencing at least a 20% delay has risen from 44% pre-2020 to 54% today. Patient recruitment, site activation, and protocol amendments remain top reasons for delays. This escalating complexity and prolonged timelines represent a significant headwind for CROs and clinical data platforms, increasing operational costs and extending time-to-market for new therapies.
forces.source_title: Clinical Trials Face Persistent Challenges—and New Opportunities

forces.title: Site Bandwidth Constraints and Operational Headaches in Clinical Trials
forces.description: Clinical trial sites are experiencing significant bandwidth constraints, with twice as many sites expecting their capacity to worsen over the next three years as expect it to improve. Key frustrations for sites include slow contracting processes and the proliferation of multiple software platforms for managing progress. These operational headaches create a substantial headwind for CROs and clinical data platforms, complicating trial execution and patient management, and necessitating better integration and streamlined processes.
forces.source_title: Clinical Trials Face Persistent Challenges—and New Opportunities

forces.title: Increasing Demand for Automated Data Collection in Clinical Trials
forces.description: There is a significant gap between the perceived importance and actual implementation of automated and passive data collection methods in clinical trials. This initiative, which directly addresses system fragmentation by digitizing paper documents and streamlining data capture across platforms, has the largest gap between 'seen' and 'wanted' by trial sites. This unmet need represents a clear upside driver for clinical data platforms and research tool providers offering integrated, efficient data management solutions to reduce site burden and improve data quality.
forces.source_title: Clinical Trials Face Persistent Challenges—and New Opportunities

forces.title: Widespread Piloting of AI Tools in Clinical Trials Underway
forces.description: A significant structural change is occurring in clinical trials, with a combined 65% of sponsors and CROs actively piloting AI tools. While full organizational redesign around AI is less common, this widespread exploration indicates a fundamental shift towards integrating AI and machine learning into research processes. This trend creates a substantial demand for AI-enabled clinical data platforms, analytical tools, and specialized CRO services that can effectively leverage these technologies to improve trial efficiency and outcomes.
forces.source_title: Clinical Trials Face Persistent Challenges—and New Opportunities

forces.title: AI-Driven Disruption in Clinical Trial Data Management
forces.description: The greatest anticipated disruption from AI in clinical trials is to data management and cleaning. Organizations still in the piloting phase largely agree on this impact, recognizing AI's potential to streamline data pipelines. This represents a structural change for clinical data platforms and CROs, shifting how data is processed and managed. While early adopters focus here, leaders are already expanding AI's role to direct trial operations and patient recruitment, signifying an evolving and deepening impact.
forces.source_title: Clinical Trials Face Persistent Challenges—and New Opportunities

forces.title: Emphasis on Workflow Redesign for AI-Powered Clinical Trial Gains
forces.description: Organizations that are taking concrete steps to redesign roles and workflows around AI capabilities in clinical trials are reporting the greatest performance gains. This indicates that merely adopting AI tools is insufficient; true value creation comes from deep integration and operational transformation. This emphasis on comprehensive redesign serves as a powerful upside driver for CROs and clinical data platforms that can offer strategic consulting and end-to-end solutions, helping clients move beyond fragmented AI implementations to truly maximize efficiency and clinical success rates.
forces.source_title: Clinical Trials Face Persistent Challenges—and New Opportunities

viewpoints.title: AI Drug Discovery Investment Misaligned with Bottlenecks in Target Identification
viewpoints.description: McKinsey believes that current AI investments in drug discovery are disproportionately concentrated in molecule design, a mature stage with clear tools. However, the true bottleneck and source of clinical failure lies in identifying and validating the correct disease mechanism. To achieve transformative breakthroughs, the industry must reallocate capital towards target identification, which requires generating and structuring proprietary biological data, not just licensing external algorithms. This shift is crucial for converting early AI gains into clinical success.
viewpoints.source_title: AI drug discovery: Focusing on what matters most

viewpoints.title: Biopharma Manufacturing Needs End-to-End Digital and AI Workflow Redesign
viewpoints.description: McKinsey argues that despite increasing investments in digital and AI, biopharma manufacturing productivity gains have plateaued since 2018, with most companies failing to scale pilot programs into operational impact. The firm asserts that the next wave of value will not come from merely adding AI to existing steps but from a fundamental redesign of work end-to-end, building connected data foundations, and automating routine activities across broader networks. This approach is essential to drive significant improvements in speed, scale, and sustainability.
viewpoints.source_title: Backbones and networks: A blueprint for the biopharma plant of the future

viewpoints.title: Clinical Trials Need AI-Driven Workflow Redesign for Substantial Performance Gains
viewpoints.description: Bain's survey reveals that while a majority of sponsors and CROs are piloting AI in clinical trials, significant performance gains are only realized by those who are actively reshaping roles and workflows around AI capabilities, not just deploying tools within existing structures. The current gap between tool adoption and organizational redesign is a defining industry characteristic. True redesign, moving beyond just data management to areas like trial monitoring and patient recruitment, is critical for addressing persistent challenges like rising complexity and delays.
viewpoints.source_title: Clinical Trials Face Persistent Challenges—and New Opportunities
